content: The text provided is a highly detailed and technical summary of various studies related to breastfeeding and its impact on health outcomes. 1. Usted et al. (2013): This study analyzed reasoning abilities in children aged 18-24 months using standardized cohort studies. The data was unadjusted and included measures of processing speed for children aged 12-18 months and 18-24 months. 2. Fonseca (2010): This study examined the prevalence of asthma in boys and girls based on breastfeeding duration. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated for breastfeeding durations of more than 12 months versus 6-12 months. Adjusted data was not provided. 3. Wong (2017): Adjusted odds ratios for allergic disorders were provided based on breastfeeding duration. Breastfeeding for 0-5 months was used as the reference group, and ORs for 6-11 months and 12-23 months were imputed. 4. Karlson (2004): Adjusted relative risks (RRs) for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) were analyzed in relation to lifetime breastfeeding duration. Data was provided for 336 out of 338 women, with RRs calculated for 4-11 months and 12-23 months of breastfeeding. No breastfeeding was the comparison group. 5. Miyake (2007): Odds ratios for wheezing episodes in the last 12 months were provided for breastfeeding durations of 7-12 months versus more than 13 months. Adjusted ORs were included, but the number of episodes was not specified. 6. Danforth (2007): This study analyzed the risk of ovarian cancer in relation to lifetime breastfeeding duration. Adjusted RRs were provided for cumulative breastfeeding durations of 12-17 months and more than 18 months, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 7. Nam (2019): Hazard ratios (HRs) for breastfeeding durations of 12-23 months versus shorter periods were imputed. Cumulative breastfeeding ORs were provided for durations of 13-18 months and 19-24 months. 8. Michels (1996): Relative risks of breast cancer were analyzed in relation to lifetime breastfeeding duration. Data was provided for 7-11 months and 12-23 months of breastfeeding, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 9. London (1990): Data was provided for cumulative breastfeeding durations of 7-11 months and 12-23 months. No breastfeeding was used as the reference group. 10. Burdette (2006): Children were classified as having high or normal adiposity based on DXA scan results. High adiposity was defined as body fat >29% for females and >24% for males. Adjusted data for overweight percentages was provided. 11. Al-Makoshi (2013): Breastfeeding data was categorized as full breastfeeding or breastfeeding cessation. Odds ratios for breastfeeding durations of more than 12 months versus 6-12 months were calculated. 12. Alho (1990): Adjusted ORs for acute otitis media and respiratory tract infections were provided for breastfeeding durations of less than 3 months versus 7-11 months and more than 12 months. 13. Stuebe (2009): Data from two NHS cohorts was combined to calculate hazard ratios for diabetes based on breastfeeding durations of 6-11 months and 12-23 months. No breastfeeding was the reference group. 14. Peters (2017): Odds ratios for cumulative breastfeeding were calculated, with 0-12 months of breastfeeding as the reference group. 15. Lee (2005): Relative risks for cumulative breastfeeding durations of 13-18 months and 19-24 months were analyzed. No breastfeeding was the reference group. 16. Gay (2015): Hazard ratios for continued and shorter breastfeeding durations were calculated, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 17. Kim (2015): Relative risks for continued and shorter breastfeeding durations were analyzed, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 18. Lupton (2013): Data for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and 18-24 months was combined to calculate odds ratios for the 12-24 month group. No breastfeeding was the reference group. 19. Natland (2012): Geometric means for HDL, LDL, triglycerides, cholesterol, and blood glucose were converted to arithmetic means. Age-stratified data was combined, with breastfeeding >24 months as the reference group. 20. Cohen (2009): Odds ratios for obesity were calculated, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 21. Zhang (2015): Odds ratios for continued and shorter breastfeeding durations were analyzed, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 22. Zhu (2020): Adjusted mean differences in IQ scores were provided for various breastfeeding durations, with breastfeeding <3 months as the reference group. 23. Daniels (2005): Adjusted mean differences for normal and low birth weight children were provided, with breastfeeding 0-6 months as the reference group. 24. Song (2020): The risk of overweight/obesity was compared between breastfeeding durations of 6-11 months and more than 12 months. The >12-month group was the reference. 25. Li (2020): Odds ratios for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and >18 months were combined using the GIV method. Breastfeeding for 12 months was the reference group. 26. Kim (2020a): Odds ratios for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and >18 months were combined. Breastfeeding for 3-6 months was the reference group. 27. Jeon (2020): Hazard ratios for continued breastfeeding versus 6-12 months were imputed, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 28. Tan (2015): Hazard ratios for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and >18 months were combined. Breastfeeding for 12 months was the reference group. 29. Gunderson (2018): Hazard ratios for continued breastfeeding (>12 months) versus 6-12 months were imputed, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 30. Tanaka (2013): Odds ratios for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and >18 months were combined. Breastfeeding for 0-6 months was the reference group. 31. Iida (2007): Odds ratios for continued breastfeeding versus 6-12 months were imputed, with 0 months of breastfeeding as the reference group. 32. Tanaka (2012): Prevalence ratios for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and >18 months were combined. Breastfeeding for <6 months was the reference group. 33. Olatosi (2014): The risk of early childhood caries (ECC) was compared between breastfeeding durations of 7-12 months and >12 months. The >12-month group was the reference. 34. Folayan (2010a): The mean dmft index for breastfeeding durations of 13-18 months and >18 months was combined for analysis. 35. Christensen (2020): Incidence rate ratios for hospitalization due to infection were provided for breastfeeding durations of 7-9 months and 10-12 months. The reference group was 0-3 months of breastfeeding. 36. Fagerhaug (2013): Data for breastfeeding durations of 7-12 months and 13-24 months was combined for analysis. The reference group was >24 months of breastfeeding. 37. Derakhshan (2017): Standard deviations were calculated from 95% confidence intervals. Data for breastfeeding durations of 13-18 months and 18-24 months was combined. 38. Ki (2017): Data for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and 18-24 months was combined. The reference group was 0-6 months of breastfeeding. 39. Yeo (2016): Data for preand post-menopausal women was combined for analysis. 40. Walby (2016): Odds ratios for continued breastfeeding (>12 months) versus 9-12 months were imputed, with never breastfeeding as the reference group. 41. Nambiar (2013): Data for male and female subjects was combined. The reference group was never breastfeeding. 42. Abarca (2019): Relative risks for continued breastfeeding (>12 months) versus 6-12 months were imputed, with never breastfeeding as the reference group. 43. Pudla (2015): Odds ratios for obesity were combined for children aged 7-10 years and 11-14 years. The reference group was never breastfeeding/<1 month. 44. Liese (2001): Odds ratios for continued breastfeeding (>12 months) versus 6-12 months were imputed, with breastfeeding <6 months as the reference group. 45. de Siqueira (2007): The risk of obesity was compared between breastfeeding durations of 6-11 months and >12 months. The >12-month group was the reference. 46. von Kries (1999): Odds ratios for continued breastfeeding (>12 months) versus 6-12 months were imputed, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 47. Haag (2019): Prevalence ratios for continued breastfeeding (12-24 months) versus <12 months were imputed, with no breastfeeding as the reference group. 48. Villamor (2000): Prevalence ratios for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and >19 months were combined. Breastfeeding for 0-6 months was the reference group. 49. Victora (2006): Adjusted means and 95% confidence intervals for lipid profiles were provided. Odds ratios for obesity were reversed for analysis. 50. Victora (1984): Data was approximated from percentage figures in the published paper. 51. Veena (2010): Data for breastfeeding durations of 12-18 months and 18-24 months was combined. Verbal fluency scores were analyzed separately for animals and first names. 52. Trygvadottir (2001): Odds ratios for continued breastfeeding (12-24 months) versus 7-12 months were imputed, with breastfeeding for 0-6 weeks as the reference group. 53. Tehrani (2014): Relative risks for continued breastfeeding (12-24 months) versus 7-12 months were imputed, with breastfeeding >24 months as the reference group. 54. Stuebe (2010): Standard deviations were derived from 95% confidence intervals. 55. Stendel-Hollis (2013): Hazard ratios for four groups of continued breastfeeding and control groups were combined. The reference group was no breastfeeding. 56. Sichieri (2003): Data for women with BMI <25 and >25, as well as nulliparous and primiparous women, was analyzed separately.
